clue.text: He's not expected to drop a brick

definitions.text: He's not expected to drop a brick

parts.words: He's not expected to drop a brick
parts.note: reads like someone trusted never to commit a social gaffe, but is literally a labourer who carries bricks up a ladder in a hod

explanation.surface: A tactful person who can be relied on never to say the wrong thing.
explanation.walkthrough: To 'drop a brick' is British slang for a tactless blunder; here it is taken literally, of the builder's mate who carries bricks.
explanation.definitionFit: A hod-carrier hauls bricks for bricklayers, so dropping them would be failing at the job.

clue.text: Standard sign of mourning

parts.note: standard reads as usual, but is a flag, lowered partway down its pole when someone dies

explanation.surface: The customary way of showing grief.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Standard' means a flag, not 'customary'.
explanation.definitionFit: A flag lowered partway down its pole marks a death.

clue.text: Favourite flower of the kennel maid?

definitions.text: Favourite flower of the kennel maid?

parts.words: Favourite flower of the kennel maid?
parts.note: a woman who looks after hounds would naturally prefer a bloom named after a canine

explanation.surface: Asking which bloom the girl who tends the dogs likes best.
explanation.definitionFit: A wild climbing briar of English hedgerows, its name prefixed with the word for a hound.

clue.text: Scourge of God

parts.note: the nickname given by Romans to the fifth-century king of the Huns who ravaged the empire

explanation.walkthrough: The '+' in the held text is a scanning blemish; the page prints 'Scourge of God'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Hun leader was called flagellum Dei, a whip sent by heaven, for his ravages.

clue.text: Wide-eyed and about fifty, this bird

indicators.note: the wide-eyed word goes about, that is around, the numeral for fifty

parts.note: staring means gazing wide-eyed
L is the Roman numeral for fifty

explanation.surface: Someone around fifty, gazing in wonder at a bird.
explanation.definitionFit: A common speckled songbird of the crow-sized family that gathers in huge flocks.

clue.text: Vehicle difficult to get out of?

definitions.text: Vehicle difficult to get out of?

parts.words: Vehicle difficult to get out of?
parts.note: a light two-wheeled horse carriage shares its name with a snare that holds its victim

explanation.surface: A car whose door sticks.
explanation.walkthrough: The word is both a pony-drawn gig and a snare.
explanation.definitionFit: A light horse-drawn cart has the same name as a device for catching animals.

clue.text: It's cruel to be without a girl

parts.note: Ruth is a girl's name
less means without, as in penniless

explanation.surface: Someone saying it is unkind to live with no girlfriend.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without' looks like a link, but supplies LESS after the girl's name.
explanation.definitionFit: Showing no pity or compassion is the core sense, a synonym.

clue.text: Tend not to be on the level

definitions.meaning: to tend towards something is to lean that way, a verb

definitions.text: not to be on the level
definitions.meaning: to slope rather than lie flat, the literal sense of leaning

explanation.surface: Someone inclined to be dishonest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not on the level' suggests dishonesty, but means literally sloping.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb covers both having a leaning towards something and physically lying at a slant.

clue.text: This paint is exclusively for exterior decoration

definitions.text: This paint is exclusively for exterior decoration

parts.words: This paint is exclusively for exterior decoration
parts.note: this word plus paint names actors' make-up, applied only to the outside of the face

explanation.surface: A decorator noting that this paint is outdoor-only.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Exterior decoration' suggests house paint; it means make-up on the face, theatrical 'greasepaint'.
explanation.definitionFit: The first half of the compound for stage make-up, an oily cosmetic worn by actors.

clue.text: But contrariwise the subject of his tale was not Bath

definitions.text: But contrariwise the subject of his tale was not Bath

parts.words: But contrariwise the subject of his tale was not Bath
parts.note: the satirist wrote A Tale of a Tub; a bath is a tub, and the town of Bath was a fashionable spa, so it was not a tale of Bath

explanation.surface: Insisting that a writer's story was not set in the spa town.
explanation.walkthrough: Jonathan Swift, Dean of St Patrick's Dublin, wrote 'A Tale of a Tub'; Bath is an English spa city.
explanation.definitionFit: The Irish satirist Jonathan Swift was dean of a Dublin cathedral and is often called by that title.

clue.text: What he gets is willingly given

definitions.text: What he gets is willingly given

parts.words: What he gets is willingly given
parts.note: the person described receives things given by will, that is left to him in a testament, not freely offered

explanation.surface: Someone who receives only what others gladly hand over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Willingly' is read as 'by will': the bequest comes through a testament.
explanation.definitionFit: One who inherits under a will receives a bequest the testator chose to leave.

clue.text: The first letter is an indefinite one

definitions.text: The first letter is an indefinite one

parts.words: The first letter is an indefinite one
parts.note: the first letter of the alphabet, A, is the grammatical indefinite part of speech placed before a noun

explanation.surface: A vague remark about the opening letter of something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Letter' suggests correspondence, but it is the alphabet's A, which grammar calls the indefinite form of this word class.
explanation.definitionFit: In grammar 'a' and 'an' are the indefinite forms of this determiner class, 'the' the definite.

clue.text: Mauretania in Yorkshire?

parts.note: Mauretania was the land of the Moors; in Yorkshire the moors are open upland heath

explanation.surface: An ocean liner of that name turning up in a northern English county.
explanation.walkthrough: Mauretania was also a famous Cunard liner, which pulls the reader to ships; the North York Moors are wild upland in the county of Yorkshire.
explanation.definitionFit: Ancient Mauretania was the homeland of the Moors, and Yorkshire is famous for its heather-covered upland heath.

clue.text: Flowers, by definition, not belonging to Flora

definitions.text: Flowers, by definition, not belonging to Flora

parts.words: Flowers, by definition, not belonging to Flora
parts.note: flowers is read as things that flow, liquids and gases, which are no part of the goddess of plants' kingdom

explanation.surface: A botanist insisting that certain blooms are not really plants.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flowers' is read as 'things that flow', not blooms; Flora is the Roman goddess of plants.
explanation.definitionFit: Liquids and gases are substances that flow, the strict sense of the word.

clue.text: The play's the answer, in hot spots

definitions.text: The play's the answer, in hot spots

parts.words: The play's the answer, in hot spots
parts.note: Arthur Miller's drama about Salem gives the name, and the plural means vessels heated to great temperatures for melting metal

explanation.surface: Echoing Hamlet's 'the play's the thing' as an answer in tight situations.
explanation.walkthrough: Arthur Miller's play 'The Crucible' supplies the word; 'hot spots' are melting pots, or severe tests.
explanation.definitionFit: Ceramic pots for melting metals at very high heat, also figuratively severe trials.

clue.text: Pace of favourites that are backed

indicators.note: backed means turned back, so the word for favourites is read from end to start

parts.note: pets are favourites, as in teacher's pets

explanation.surface: The speed of racing favourites that punters have backed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Backed' suggests betting on favourites; here it means turned backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: A pace is a single stride, as is a footstep.

clue.text: Thrustful fellows

parts.note: reads as pushy, ambitious men, but means men who thrust with a blade

explanation.definitionFit: Fencers and duellists fight by lunging, thrusting a blade at an opponent.

clue.text: Miles of American poetry

parts.note: miles reads as a great length of verse, but is the first name of a Pilgrim captain in a Longfellow poem

explanation.surface: Endless lengths of American verse.
explanation.walkthrough: Longfellow's 'The Courtship of Miles Standish' is about the Plymouth colony's military captain.
explanation.definitionFit: Captain Myles Standish of Plymouth Colony is the hero of Longfellow's narrative poem.

clue.text: Slow-growing plants?

parts.note: plants that grow along slowly are pictured as moving at a crawl, like someone tiptoeing

explanation.definitionFit: Vines that trail along the ground or walls are named for moving slowly and stealthily.

clue.text: Not what is meant by turning the other cheek

definitions.text: Not what is meant by turning the other cheek

parts.words: Not what is meant by turning the other cheek
parts.note: turning the other cheek means meekly accepting a blow; a complete turnabout of opinion is a different kind of turning

explanation.surface: A reminder that the Gospel phrase does not mean what someone thinks.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase from the Sermon on the Mount is about forgiveness; the answer is a complete reversal of position, borrowed from French.
explanation.definitionFit: An about-turn is a sudden reversal of policy or opinion.

clue.text: Ran into both ways in Italy

indicators.note: both ways means the word from into is written backwards before and forwards after

parts.note: to can mean into, as in went to town
taken as written
the same word to, now read forwards

explanation.surface: Bumping into someone, going in both directions, somewhere in Italy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'into' does double duty as a word for 'to', and 'both ways' asks for it read backwards and forwards round RAN; 'in Italy' marks the answer as a place there.
explanation.definitionFit: A port town on the heel of the Italian peninsula, an example of a place there.

clue.text: Box in wooden fashion

parts.note: box is the verb to fight with fists, as in practice bouts, and also hints at a timber pole

explanation.surface: Fighting stiffly, like a boxer with no grace.
explanation.walkthrough: One word covers both senses: to box in a practice bout, and a stout wooden pole on a ship.
explanation.definitionFit: To exchange practice punches is the verb; the noun is a pole such as a mast or boom.

clue.text: A 5 for the unwary miner ?

parts.note: 5 down is a snare; for a miner the snare would be a fall down a shaft

explanation.surface: A danger waiting for a careless coal-miner.
explanation.walkthrough: The cross-reference is to 5 down, a snare; a miner works in a pit.
explanation.definitionFit: A hidden danger or snare, literally a covered hole one drops into.

clue.text: How some strikers are put out

definitions.text: How some strikers are put out

parts.words: How some strikers are put out
parts.note: strikers suggests workers on strike, but in cricket the batsman facing is the striker, dismissed when a fielder holds the ball

explanation.surface: How some industrial strikers are dismissed.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket the batsman receiving the ball is 'the striker'; he is out if a fielder holds his shot before it lands.
explanation.definitionFit: A cricket dismissal where a fielder holds the hit ball before it bounces.

clue.text: He has winning ways

parts.note: winning ways usually means charm, but here means the habit of coming first

explanation.surface: A charming man.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Winning ways' means charm; here it means one who wins.
explanation.definitionFit: The winner of a contest is the one who triumphs.

clue.text: Original habits

parts.note: habits as clothing, and original as belonging to Adam and Eve, who sewed fig leaves into the first garments

explanation.surface: Customs that are fresh and inventive.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Habits' means garments, as a monk's habit; Genesis says Adam and Eve sewed fig leaves into the first ones.
explanation.definitionFit: In the King James Genesis, the first humans made themselves fig-leaf coverings for the waist.

clue.text: The spirit is in the basin, perhaps

indicators.note: perhaps signals that the letters of the basin are only one possible order, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A ghost lurking in the washbasin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spirit' suggests a ghost, but it is a drink; 'perhaps' asks for THEBASIN to be rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: A strong green aniseed liqueur flavoured with wormwood is a distilled spirit.

clue.text: French version of "The Lady of the Lake"?

definitions.text: French version of "The Lady of the Lake"?

parts.words: French version of "The Lady of the Lake"?
parts.note: the French for mother is a lady's title, and the English word spelt the same means a small lake

explanation.surface: Asking for a French translation of Scott's poem.
explanation.walkthrough: French 'mère' is mother, a lady; English 'mere' is a lake.
explanation.definitionFit: In English a small lake or pond; in French the same letters mean a mother.

clue.text: Assault by battery

parts.note: assault and battery is a legal term, but here a battery is a unit of artillery attacking

explanation.surface: A legal charge of assault and battery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Assault and battery' is the familiar legal charge; in the army a battery is a group of big guns.
explanation.definitionFit: An artillery battery attacks by shooting its cannon.

clue.text: Reds eat out on the platform

indicators.note: out means put out of order, so the letters of reds eat are rearranged

explanation.surface: Communists eating outside on a stage.
explanation.definitionFit: A dais or raised stage is a slightly raised floor for a speaker.

clue.text: Tokens of success for 24s

parts.note: 24 down is the winner, so these are what winners are given

explanation.surface: Badges of achievement handed to the champions.
explanation.definitionFit: Cups and shields are awarded to winners as signs of their success.

clue.text: Bores show the doctor their complaints

parts.note: Dr is the abbreviation for doctor
ills are ailments or complaints

explanation.surface: Tedious people telling the doctor about their ailments.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bores' looks like tedious people, but is a verb: makes holes.
explanation.definitionFit: To bore a hole is to use a tool that cuts by rotation, a synonym.
